q: "Illam meae si partem anima tulit Maturior vis, quid moror altera? Nec carus aeque, nec superstes Integer? Ille dies utramque Duxit ruinam." ["If that half of my soul were snatch away from me by an untimely stroke, why should the other stay? That which remains will not be equally dear, will not be whole: the same day will involve the destruction of both."] or: ["If a superior force has taken that part of my soul, why do I, the remaining one, linger behind? What is left is not so dear, nor an entire thing: this day has wrought the destruction of both." —Horace, Ode, ii. 17, 5.]
"Quis desiderio sit pudor, aut modus Tam cari capitis?" ["What shame can there, or measure, in lamenting so dear a friend?" —Horace, Ode, i. 24, I.]
“Quis puer ocius Restinguet ardentis Falerni Pocula praetereunte lympha?” [“What boy will quickly come and cool the heat of the Falernian wine with clear water?”—Horace, Od., ii. z, 18.]
"Paulum sepultae distat inertiae Celata virtus:" ["Virtue concealed little differs from dead sloth." —Horace, Od., iv. 9, 29.]

"Sic tauriformis volvitur Aufidus; Qui regna Dauni perfluit Appuli, Dum saevit, horrendamque cultis Diluviem meditatur agris;" ["So the biforked Aufidus, which flows through the realm of the Apulian Daunus, when raging, threatens a fearful deluge to the tilled ground."—Horat., Od., iv. 14, 25.]

"Narras et genus AEaci, Et pugnata sacro bella sub Ilio Quo Chium pretio cadum Mercemur, quis aquam temperet ignibus, Quo praebente domum, et quota, Pelignis caream frigoribus, taces." ["You tell us long stories about the race of AEacus, and the battles fought under sacred Ilium; but what to give for a cask of Chian wine, who shall prepare the warm bath, and in whose house, and when I may escape from the Pelignian cold, you do not tell us." —Horace, Od., iii. 19, 3.]

“Num tu, qux tenuit dives Achaemenes, Aut pinguis Phrygiae Mygdonias opes, Permutare velis crine Licymnim? Plenas aut Arabum domos, Dum fragrantia detorquet ad oscula Cervicem, aut facili sxvitia negat, Quae poscente magis gaudeat eripi, Interdum rapere occupet?” [“Wouldst thou not exchange all that the wealthy Arhaemenes had, or the Mygdonian riches of fertile Phrygia, for one ringlet of Licymnia’s hair? or the treasures of the Arabians, when she turns her head to you for fragrant kisses, or with easily assuaged anger denies them, which she would rather by far you took by force, and sometimes herself snatches one!”—Horace, Od., ii. 12, 21.]
[ Many brave men lived before Agamemnon, but all are pressed by the long night unmourned and unknown."—Horace, Od., iv. 9, 25.]

“Aut verberatae grandine vineae, Fundusque mendax, arbore nunc aquas Culpante, nunc torrentia agros Sidera, nunc hyemes iniquas.” [“Or hail-smitten vines and the deceptive farm...”—Horatius, Od., iii. 1, 29.]

"Eheu! cicatricum, et sceleris pudet, Fratrumque: quid nos dura refugimus AEtas? quid intactum nefasti Liquimus? Unde manus inventus Metu Deorum continuit? quibus Pepercit aris." ["Alas! our crimes and our fratricides are a shame to us! What crime does this bad age shrink from? What wickedness have we left undone? What youth is restrained from evil by the fear of the gods? What altar is spared?"—Horace, Od., i. 33, 35]

"Quanto quisque sibi plum negaverit, A diis plum feret: nil cupientium Nudus castra peto . . . . Multa petentibus Desunt multa." ["The more each man denies himself, the more the gods give him. Poor as I am, I seek the company of those who ask nothing; they who desire much will be deficient in much." —Horace, Od., iii. 16,21,42.]
"Nihil supra Deos lacesso." ["I trouble the gods no farther."—Horace, Od., ii. 18, 11.]
"Jure perhorrui Lath conspicuum tollere verticem." ["I ever justly feared to raise my head too high." —Horace, Od.,iii. 16, 18.]
"Mista senum et juvenum densentur funera; nullum Saeva caput Proserpina fugit;" ["Old and young die in mixed heaps. Cruel Proserpine forbears none."—Horace, Od., i. 28, 19.]
"Et militavi non sine gloria;" ["And I have played the soldier not ingloriously." —Horace, Od., iii. 26, 2.]

q: “Chi puo dir com’ egli arde, a in picciol fuoco,” [“He who can say how he burns with love, has little fire” —Petrarca, Sonetto 137.]

"E cosi avven, the l’animo ciascuna Sua passion sotto ‘l contrario manto, Ricopre, con la vista or’chiara, or’bruna." ["And thus it happens that the mind of each veils its passion under a different appearance, and beneath a smiling visage, gay beneath a sombre air."—Petrarch.]

I observe that the best of the ancient poets have avoided affectation and the hunting after, not only fantastic Spanish and Petrarchic elevations, but even the softer and more gentle touches, which are the ornament of all succeeding poesy.
"Ne si, ne no, nel cor mi suona intero." ["My heart does not tell me either yes or no."—Petrarch.]

q: And, besides, they have a very advantageous way of making use of all sorts of events: for what fortune, nature, or any other cause (of which the number is infinite), products of good and healthful in us, it is the privilege of physic to attribute to itself; all the happy successes that happen to the patient, must be thence derived; the accidents that have cured me, and a thousand others, who do not employ physicians, physicians usurp to themselves: and as to ill accidents, they either absolutely disown them, in laying the fault upon the patient, by such frivolous reasons as they are never at a loss for; as “he lay with his arms out of bed,” or “he was disturbed with the rattling of a coach:” “Rhedarum transitus arcto Vicorum inflexu:” [“The passage of the wheels in the narrow turning of the street”—Juvenal, iii. 236.] or “somebody had set open the casement,” or “he had lain upon his left side,” or “he had some disagreeable fancies in his head”: in sum, a word, a dream, or a look, seems to them excuse sufficient wherewith to palliate their own errors: or, if they so please, they even make use of our growing worse, and do their business in this way which can never fail them: which is by buzzing us in the ear, when the disease is more inflamed by their medicaments, that it had been much worse but for those remedies; he, whom from an ordinary cold they have thrown into a double tertian-ague, had but for them been in a continued fever. They do not much care what mischief they do, since it turns to their own profit. In earnest, they have reason to require a very favourable belief from their patients; and, indeed, it ought to be a very easy one, to swallow things so hard to be believed. q: and throughout his brief life his beau idéal remained Rupert Brooke, whose biography he hoped one day to write.

q: in 1960 he wrote a short book on Racine, which scandalized academic critics
c: Susan Sontag mentions Barthes's polemical short book on Racine, which caused a scandal among academic critics.

q: Sophocles’ Ajax
c: Susan Sontag notes that a student of Pašović would be directing Sophocles' play, highlighting the continuation of classical theatre in wartime Sarajevo.

q: we marvel at a Nabokov, a Beckett, a Cabrera Infante
c: Sontag cites Cabrera Infante as an example of a modern writer with the virtuosity to write brilliant prose in more than one language.

q: An older, milder refusal is lodged in the French skeptic tradition from Montaigne to Gide
Barthes is the latest major participant in the great national literary project, inaugurated by Montaigne: the self as vocation, life as a reading of the self.

The elaboration of the garden grotto, a principal feature of the new heights attained by the garden in the Renaissance, produced such triumphs as the Grotta Grande in the Medici’s Boboli Gardens in Florence and the many grottoes and hydraulic marvels of Pratolino, so admired by Montaigne and other foreign visitors.
c: Susan Sontag references Montaigne as part of a French skeptical tradition that influences Barthes's aversion to rigid systems.
Susan Sontag identifies Montaigne as the inaugurator of a French literary project focused on the self, in which Barthes is a later participant.
Susan Sontag mentions that Montaigne admired the grottoes and hydraulic marvels at Pratolino during his travels.

q: Montaigne’s Essays
c: Susan Sontag references Montaigne's Essays as a classic of autobiography that includes a prologue addressing the reader's potential scruples about self-writing.

q: Jean Paul, Franz Grillparzer, Adalbert Stifter, Robert Walser, the Hofmannsthal of “The Lord Chandos Letter,” Thomas Bernhard are a few of the affiliations of this contemporary master of the literature of lament and of mental restlessness.
c: Susan Sontag lists Jean Paul as part of a German literary genealogy that informs the style and themes of the writer being discussed.

q: Enjoying the impertinent energy and wit of a species of performance called Happenings did not make me care less about Aristotle and Shakespeare.
c: Susan Sontag mentions Aristotle as a canonical figure whose work she continued to admire despite her interest in contemporary art.

q: Much of barthes’s work is devoted to the repertoire of pleasure—"the great adventure of desire," as he calls it in the essay on Brillat-Savarin’s Physiology of Taste.
c: Susan Sontag references Barthes's essay on Brillat-Savarin's book as an example of his focus on pleasure and desire.

q: and Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby.
c: Susan Sontag cites this novel as another work featuring a shadowy bachelor narrator who observes more reckless characters.

q: which runs from Sterne through, in our own century, Natsume Soseki’s I Am a Cat
c: Susan Sontag includes this book in a tradition of narrative buffoonery and talkative first-person narration.

q: The instrumental view expounded in Sartre’s What Is Literature? (1948) makes of literature something perpetually obsolete, a vain—and misplaced—struggle between ethical good soldiers and literary purists, that is, modernists.
c: Susan Sontag critiques Sartre's view of literature as presented in his book 'What Is Literature?', describing it as instrumental and leading to a conformist sentiment.

q: the love recounted in his one perfect book, The Words
c: Susan Sontag refers to Sartre's book 'The Words' as a perfect account of his love for literature.

q: Visconti’s first film, Ossessione—adapted from James M. Cain’s The Postman Always Kings Twice—is a far nobler achievement than his handsome, respectful transcription of The Leopard or his stiff, rather absent version of Camus’s The Stranger.
c: Susan Sontag references James M. Cain's novel 'The Postman Always Rings Twice' as the source for Visconti's film 'Ossessione', comparing it favorably to adaptations of literary classics.

q: the opening chapter, a brilliant exercise in Brief-Life writing which recounts the biography of the much-traveled Stendhal
c: Susan Sontag references Stendhal as a biographical subject in Sebald's work, noting Sebald's recounting of his life as an exercise in 'Brief-Life writing'.

q: when Kate Chopin published The Awakening
c: Susan Sontag references Chopin's novel 'The Awakening' to place the photographs within a specific cultural and historical moment, noting the controversial reception of such works.

q: Jean Paul, Franz Grillparzer, Adalbert Stifter, Robert Walser, the Hofmannsthal of “The Lord Chandos Letter,” Thomas Bernhard are a few of the affiliations of this contemporary master of the literature of lament and of mental restlessness.
c: Susan Sontag references Hofmannsthal specifically through his work 'The Lord Chandos Letter,' placing him in a German literary tradition.

q: The Egoist
c: Susan Sontag references this novel as an example of a work that uses essayistic digressions to plump out the story.

Susan Sontag lists Thomas Bernhard as part of a German literary genealogy that informs the style and themes of the writer being discussed.

q: Sebald is the writer who plays most daringly with this project now.
c: Susan Sontag identifies Sebald as a contemporary writer who boldly experiments with blending factual and fictional elements in his narratives.

q: The distraught heroine of Don DeLillo’s The Body Artist logs on to her computer at odd hours to watch a live-streaming video feed from the edge of a two-lane road outside Kotka, Finland, where a webcam is always trained on asphalt.
c: Susan Sontag cites this novel as an example of modern, solitary travel through technology, contrasting it with Halliburton's immersive travel.

q: (The affecting fantasia of Hesse’s Steppenwolf seems, in comparison, riddled with sentimentality.)
c: Susan Sontag contrasts Ferdydurke with Hesse's Steppenwolf, noting that the latter appears sentimental in comparison.

q: Giotto or van Eyck
c: Susan Sontag references van Eyck as one of the 'great, innocent artists of the past' in a rhetorical question about artistic response to contemporary flaws.

q: Rousseau’s Confessions
c: Susan Sontag cites Rousseau's Confessions as an example of a spiritually ambitious autobiographical work with a defensive prologue.

q: Rousseau offers another ideal—passionate, avowing vulnerability.
c: Susan Sontag references Rousseau as providing an alternative ideal of self-absorption, characterized by passion and vulnerability, in contrast to Valéry's impersonal approach.

q: Another of Machado’s models was a marvelous book by Xavier de Maistre, a French expatriate aristocrat (he lived most of his long life in Russia) who invented the literary micro-journey with his Journey around My Room
c: Susan Sontag identifies this book as another direct model for Machado de Assis, describing its invention of the literary micro-journey.

q: Kiš had a complicated literary genealogy, which he was undoubtedly simplifying when he declared himself, as he often did, a child of Borges and of Bruno Schulz.

q: PYRAMUS: Goethe said—

q: Wagner had predicted to Mathilde Wesendonk while composing the last act, is “bound to drive people mad.”

q: his second book—it appeared in 1954—which is on Michelet.
c: Susan Sontag notes that Barthes's second book was a study of the historian Michelet, analyzing his metaphors and themes.

q: in the writings of Nietzsche, Pater, Wilde, Ortega (the Ortega of “The Dehumanization of Art”), and James Joyce.
c: Susan Sontag cites Ortega, specifically referencing his essay 'The Dehumanization of Art,' as a source for the aesthete's point of view she embraced.

q: But what about when the “I” and the author bear the same name or have identical life circumstances, as in Sleepless Nights, or in V. S. Naipaul’s The Enigma of Arrival and W. G. Sebald’s Vertigo?
c: Susan Sontag includes Sebald's book as another example of a narrative where Susan Sontag and narrator share a name, exploring the fusion of fact and fiction.

q: Jasper Johns, explaining something about “my general development so far,” said: “That is to say, I find it more interesting to use a real fork as a painting than it is to use a painting as a real fork.”
c: Susan Sontag quotes Jasper Johns to illustrate a point about the fork as an emblem of the real, using his statement to contrast artistic representation with utility.

q: The Socratic sweetness and charm become more plaintive, more desperate: writing is an embrace, a being embraced; every idea is an idea reaching out.

—CHIKAMATSU MONZAEMON (1653–1725)

In order to make the art of the puppets competitive with the art of living actors, says Chikamatsu, the text must be “charged with feeling.” But, he adds, “I take pathos to be entirely a matter of restraint.”

q: "Everywhere and at all times," Lévi-Strauss has observed, "the European code of politeness rules out the possibility of eating noisily."
c: Susan Sontag cites Lévi-Strauss's observation on European dining etiquette to contrast with the informal, gooey experience of eating marshmallows.

q: Sylvia Plath
c: Susan Sontag cites Plath's texts as part of the collage in Pašović's production, demonstrating the incorporation of modern poetry into Sarajevo's theatre.
